parts.note: in Sean O'Casey's play Juno and the Paycock, Juno's partner is Captain Boyle, the 'Paycock', an Irish way of saying the bird with the fanned tail; the clue asks for the adjective meaning like that bird

explanation.surface: A classical query about whom the queen of the gods was paired with in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Juno suggests the Roman goddess, whose sacred bird was the peacock, but the drama is O'Casey's Juno and the Paycock, set in Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Latin pavo, a peacock, so it means resembling that showy bird, the Paycock of the play.

parts.note: a London costermonger's leader who wears clothes sewn all over with mother-of-pearl buttons

explanation.surface: A monarch of buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pearly King is a Cockney charity figure whose suit is covered in shiny buttons; the answer is the first word of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: London's costermonger kings wear suits covered in mother-of-pearl buttons, giving them their title.

parts.note: a single word precedes both 'Fair', as in Thackeray's novel, and 'case', a small bag for cosmetics

explanation.surface: A question about whether a legal argument is just.
explanation.walkthrough: Case suggests a lawsuit and fair a just one; in fact the word goes before both: Thackeray's Vanity Fair and a make-up case.
explanation.definitionFit: The word joins Thackeray's novel title and also names a small toiletries bag.

parts.note: the clue describes a symbol that itself stands for zero

explanation.surface: Someone looks in a box and finds it empty.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a report of emptiness, but it defines the figure for zero.
explanation.definitionFit: This written figure, a cipher, represents zero, an absence of any quantity.

parts.note: Harwell in Oxfordshire was Britain's atomic energy research establishment, suggesting atomic nuclei; the word means having a central nucleolus

explanation.surface: A question about what is based at a research site.
explanation.walkthrough: Harwell was the UK Atomic Energy Research Establishment, so the clue evokes nuclear science; the answer is a biological term for having a nucleolus.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology the word describes a cell or nucleus containing a small central body, a nucleolus, so it is centred.

parts.note: Sir John ... was a 17th-century English poet, and the village in Buckinghamshire sharing his surname housed famous British film studios

explanation.surface: A poet who works in a film studio.
explanation.walkthrough: One name serves both: the poet of Cooper's Hill and the Buckinghamshire village whose film studios made many classic British pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of a Stuart-era poet is also the place name of well-known British film studios.

clue.text: Proceeds to put a name up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the whole run of pieces is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to set something is to put it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone goes ahead and posts a name on a board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proceeds' looks like money taken, but it is the verb; 'up' applies to the whole phrase, read from bottom to top in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue or flow out from a source is to proceed from it.

indicators.note: uncertain says the letters of the two words are in no fixed order

explanation.surface: Something whose zero setting is unpredictable is dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncertain' rearranges WITH and ZERO; the definition is the noun sense, a piece of explosive ordnance.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-barrelled artillery gun firing shells at high angles, so loosely an explosive weapon.

clue.text: Make the most of the latest fashion

definitions.text: Make the most of the latest fashion

parts.words: Make the most of the latest fashion
parts.note: the clue reads both as make the most of something and as make into the long 'maxi' style, the fashion of the day

explanation.surface: Advice to take full advantage of current trends.
explanation.walkthrough: When the clue was set, the maxi skirt was the latest fashion; the verb can be read as making something maxi.
explanation.definitionFit: To increase something to its greatest possible extent is to make the most of it.

clue.text: Say, is Ann putting on weight ?

indicators.note: putting on means the next piece is added straight after the name, as weight is added to a body

parts.note: taken as written, a girl's name
an ounce is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Ann has been gaining weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like an introductory 'for instance' but it is the verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare or proclaim something publicly is to state it, a synonym of say.

clue.text: Call for a truce with anger? Some neck!

parts.note: pax is the schoolboy call for a truce, from Latin for peace
wax is an old British word for a fit of anger, as in 'in a wax'

explanation.surface: Someone calls a truce while still angry, which takes some nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some neck!' sounds like an exclamation at cheek, but it defines a ligament of the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the strong elastic ligament running down the back of the neck in grazing animals, so it is part of a neck.

parts.note: majority here means coming of age at 21, traditionally marked by being given the key of the door; the symbol is now old-fashioned

explanation.surface: A question about a political emblem that has gone out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: Majority suggests the larger party or voting bloc, but here it is legal adulthood, once celebrated with a front-door key.
explanation.definitionFit: Being handed one's own front-door key was the traditional token of reaching adulthood at twenty-one.

clue.text: Diet at morning keeps the little chap in good shape

parts.note: to bant is to diet, from William Banting's slimming regime
AM, ante meridiem, is morning

explanation.surface: A morning diet keeps a small man fit.
explanation.walkthrough: To bant, after the Victorian slimmer William Banting, is an old word for dieting.
explanation.definitionFit: A small but plucky fighting fowl gives the word for a small, spirited person, also a boxing weight class.

parts.note: sky-signs suggests illuminated advertising high on buildings, but means the zodiac signs read in the heavens

explanation.surface: A specialist in rooftop neon advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: A sky-sign is also an illuminated advertisement on a rooftop; here it is a sign of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who interprets stars and planets as omens reads the signs of the zodiac.

parts.note: white-coat suggests doctors or laboratory staff, but these tradesmen coat walls in white

explanation.surface: Laboratory or hospital staff in white coats.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious reading is scientists or doctors in white coats; instead 'coat' is a verb, applying a white coat to walls.
explanation.definitionFit: These tradesmen spread a smooth layer of lime or gypsum mix over walls and ceilings.

clue.text: Tottenham players hold a promissory note; it's false!

indicators.note: hold means the first piece contains the second

parts.note: Tottenham Hotspur, the London football club, are known as Spurs
an IOU is a written promise to pay

explanation.surface: Footballers holding an IOU find it is a forgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Tottenham Hotspur is a north London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Something counterfeit or not genuine is false.

parts.note: the music-hall song 'Has Anybody Here Seen Kelly?' calls him Kelly from the Isle of Man, whose judges have a special title

explanation.surface: A question about the magistrate in Kelly's case.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song names 'Kelly from the Isle of Man', and a judge of the Manx courts has a distinctive title.
explanation.definitionFit: The two senior judges of the Isle of Man bear this title, so a Manxman like Kelly would come before one.

clue.text: Performed to Handel's Water Music presumably

definitions.text: Performed to Handel's Water Music presumably

parts.words: Performed to Handel's Water Music presumably
parts.note: water comes from a tap, so a dance performed to water music is read as a dance of the tap

explanation.surface: A ballet staged to Handel's famous orchestral suite.
explanation.walkthrough: Tap, the source of water, plus dance gives a step dance with metal-heeled shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhythmic step dance in shoes with metal plates is danced to music, and 'tap' links it to water.

clue.text: Rhymesters who dip into Edgar Allan?

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer
people who dip into food or books to sample them are tasters

explanation.surface: Poets who sample the works of Edgar Allan Poe.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces read together as those who sample Poe, which is how the surface plays it.
explanation.definitionFit: A petty, inferior poet is a mere versifier, a rhymester.

clue.text: " If they run, why, we follow, and run 'em (Garrick)

definitions.text: If they run, why, we follow, and run 'em

parts.words: If they run, why, we follow, and run 'em
parts.note: the line is from David Garrick's song Heart of Oak, about chasing enemy ships until they are driven onto land

explanation.surface: A line from a naval song completed by the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: David Garrick wrote the words of Heart of Oak, the Royal Navy's march; the line ends with enemy ships driven aground.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means onto the shore or dry land, where fleeing ships are driven.

clue.text: Shut in, so I am wan

parts.note: I'm is the contraction of I am
wan means pale

explanation.surface: Someone confined indoors notices how pallid they look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut in' is not an invalid but the old verb meaning to enclose with a fence of pales.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaically the verb means to enclose or fence in with stakes, so to shut in.

parts.note: The Tinted Venus is an 1885 comic novel by the Victorian humorist who wrote Vice Versa

explanation.surface: An artist's statue of Venus was coloured.
explanation.walkthrough: F. Anstey, pen name of Thomas Anstey Guthrie, wrote The Tinted Venus, in which a statue of the goddess comes to life.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian humorist's pen name is the answer, the author of The Tinted Venus.

parts.note: the quotation is John Bright's line on Ireland, the missing word being a cure

explanation.surface: A Victorian statesman's dictum on the use of force.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bright, the 19th-century British radical, said 'Force is not a remedy' in a speech on Ireland in 1880; the solver completes the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the quotation means a cure or corrective.

parts.note: Rugby is the English public school, and its famous bully is the tormentor in Tom Brown's School Days

explanation.surface: A rough player on the rugby field.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby looks like the sport, but it is Rugby School, setting of Thomas Hughes's novel, whose bully later starred in George MacDonald Fraser's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Flashman is the cowardly tormentor of Tom Brown in Thomas Hughes's novel of school life.

indicators.note: the letters of the next two words are taken in a new arrangement, as if in play

explanation.surface: A lively dance step in the first act of a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited' refers to motor spirit, petrol; the letters of ACT and ONE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An octane rating measures the anti-knock quality of petrol, which British English calls motor spirit.

clue.text: Ranting wildly about nothing is just uninformed

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the next piece
wildly says the letters of ranting are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: O, the round figure, is nothing

explanation.surface: Raving about nothing shows someone does not know the facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' turns RANTING into IGNRANT, and 'about' puts it around O.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking knowledge or information is uninformed.

parts.note: an English home county whose name is also a light four-wheeled carriage that a horse would pull

explanation.surface: A question about which English county has a famous white horse carved on a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: Chalk white horses suggest Berkshire or Wiltshire; the county meant is the one that is also a horse-drawn carriage, just south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: This county south of London also names a light American horse-drawn carriage.

parts.note: Bunthorne in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience is 'a ...-yallery, Grosvenor Gallery, foot-in-the-grave young man'; the missing word rhymes with yallery

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank line from a Gilbert and Sullivan patter song.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Patience (1881), mocking aesthetes; the blank is the word paired with 'yallery', an affected form of yellow.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means foliage, plants seen as a mass of green colour.
